raw_comment:
It all points to awesome to me…

    Isn’t it awesome that in much of this world we have:
    - Birth control that gives women the ability to choose when and how many children to have 
    - Much reduced childhood mortality that means fewer children are necessary to ensure some will survive to become adults 
    - Greater educational opportunities and social freedoms for women, who may now choose their life’s path, rather than have it forced upon them 
    - population growth that is leveling out… I have little doubt we would eventually kill ourselves off if we grew unchecked. 
    
    The only downside? We will need to figure our way out of the economic ponzi scheme the modern markets have set up, that relies on ever increasing and expanding consumerism to not collapse.

raw_comment:
Obviously, this is not news. There were reports and coverage on this topic over 20 years ago. 
    
    A UN report published in 2012 highlighted “…A significant factor, is that many people cannot have the number of children they want due to financial hardship, lack of quality healthcare, and societal barriers, rather than a lack of desire for children.”
    
    Birth rates have declined worldwide due to:
    
    1. women's improved education and access to jobs
    2. lower child mortality (fewer babies needed for family survival)
    3. rising costs of raising children
    4. better access to contraception
    5. increased urbanization (less farm labor needed)
    6. delayed marriage
    7. changing cultural values prioritizing careers and personal fulfillment over large families
    8. societal & future concerns with anxiety about climate change, economic instability, and political issues
    
    Sorry, no conspiracies, no nefariousness. So, what are we going to do to make it less expensive for folks to have and raise children?

raw_comment:
The decrease in the birth rate is due to human exposure to synthetic chemicals. 
    
    Sperm count is declining at an accelerated place globally. 
    
    Known and suspected endocrine disrupting chemicals are widespread due to our use of cosmetics and personal care products, pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, industrial chemicals, and metals (lead, cadmium, mercury, and arsenic are in paint and water pipelines, cigarette smoking, industrial emissions, fertilizers; coal burning; herbicides, fossil fuels). Biomonitoring studies continue to report routine human exposures to hundreds or thousands of chemicals. 
    
    The health outcomes in men, for example, are prostate cancer, testicular cancer, male infertility and sub fertility (sperm decline), hypogonadism (low testosterone), sexual dysfunctions, and intergenerational effects. 
    
    One in every 8 women will develop breast cancer during their lifetime, and it has to do with endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs). Science shows us how pesticide exposure impacts cancer aggressiveness and tumor immunopathology mechanisms.  
    
    Overall, human fertility is reduced.

raw_comment: The dominant impression is that fertility rates have declined sharply and consistently across nearly all regions since the 1960s, converging toward or below replacement level. The United States, once well above two children per woman, has steadily fallen to European levels, while even historically high-fertility regions such as Mexico and much of Africa show long-term downward trajectories. Israel is a clear outlier, maintaining a notably higher and more stable fertility rate compared with other high-income countries.

raw_comment:
It all points to awesome to me…
    
    Isn’t it awesome that in much of this world we have:
    - Birth control that gives women the ability to choose when and how many children to have 
    - Much reduced childhood mortality that means fewer children are necessary to ensure some will survive to become adults 
    - Greater educational opportunities and social freedoms for women, who may now choose their life’s path, rather than have it forced upon them 
    - population growth that is leveling out… I have little doubt we would eventually kill ourselves off if we grew unchecked. 
    
    The only downside? We will need to figure our way out of the economic ponzi scheme the modern markets have set up, that relies on ever increasing and expanding consumerism to not collapse.

raw_comment:
Obviously, this is not news. There were reports and coverage on this topic over 20 years ago. 
    
    A UN report published in 2012 highlighted “…A significant factor, is that many people cannot have the number of children they want due to financial hardship, lack of quality healthcare, and societal barriers, rather than a lack of desire for children.”
    
    Birth rates have declined worldwide due to:
    
    1. women's improved education and access to jobs
    2. lower child mortality (fewer babies needed for family survival)
    3. rising costs of raising children
    4. better access to contraception
    5. increased urbanization (less farm labor needed)
    6. delayed marriage
    7. changing cultural values prioritizing careers and personal fulfillment over large families
    8. societal & future concerns with anxiety about climate change, economic instability, and political issues
    
    Sorry, no conspiracies, no nefariousness. So, what are we going to do to make it less expensive for folks to have and raise children?

raw_comment:
The decrease in the birth rate is due to human exposure to synthetic chemicals. 
    
    Sperm count is declining at an accelerated place globally. 
    
    Known and suspected endocrine disrupting chemicals are widespread due to our use of cosmetics and personal care products, pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, industrial chemicals, and metals (lead, cadmium, mercury, and arsenic are in paint and water pipelines, cigarette smoking, industrial emissions, fertilizers; coal burning; herbicides, fossil fuels). Biomonitoring studies continue to report routine human exposures to hundreds or thousands of chemicals. 
    
    The health outcomes in men, for example, are prostate cancer, testicular cancer, male infertility and sub fertility (sperm decline), hypogonadism (low testosterone), sexual dysfunctions, and intergenerational effects. 
    
    One in every 8 women will develop breast cancer during their lifetime, and it has to do with endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs). Science shows us how pesticide exposure impacts cancer aggressiveness and tumor immunopathology mechanisms.  
    
    Overall, human fertility is reduced.

raw_comment:
WHAT DO I NOTICE?
    
    I notice that birth rates have been declining in the past 65 years, with rates varying from nation to nation. European countries and the United States for example, have a higher decreasing rate than nations in the Middle East and Africa.
    
    WHAT DO I WONDER?
    
    I wonder why the rates have decreased. Is it because of climate change, cultural differences, or rapidly changing technology? Personally, I believe it is a mix of all three, with the shifting environment and economy as the most significant factor. 
    
    HOW DOES THIS RELATE TO MY COMMUNITY?
    
    
    This mainly relates to my generation. As society moves forward, the birth rates only seem to drop more. There is microplastic being found in blood, it was scorching hot in October, and people can barely afford to live in a tight apartment. I don’t mean to be so bleak, but given the hostile environment that the past generations have set up, who can blame my generation for not wanting to have kids? 
    
    HEADLINE:
    THE BABY DIP! THE “BOOM” HAS LONG PASSED US!

    The Drastic Decline in Birth Rates Worldwide

The current world economy is utterly dependent on growth or it stagnates. 
    
    All countries face a decline in birth rates, but for different reasons.     Examining the current US economy gives some huge clues.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that fertility rates have been steadily declining across almost all regions of the world since 1960. Countries like the U.S., France, Canada, and Norway all dropped from above 3 children per woman to around or below 2. Some regions, especially Central & Western Africa, still have higher fertility rates, but even those show a downward trend.
    2. I wonder why fertility rates dropped so dramatically across so many places. Is it due to economic changes, cultural shifts, women’s education, urbanization, cost of living, or access to contraception?
    3. In many communities today—including mine—people are having fewer children because of financial pressure, busy work lifestyles, and a desire for career stability. Many young adults feel that raising kids is expensive and challenging.
    4. From Boom to Decline: Fertility Rates Fall Worldwide

raw_comment:
Looking at this graph, I see that birth rates have dropped a lot worldwide since 1960. Most countries, like the U.S., France, and Canada, now have fewer than two children per woman. Israel is one of the few countries with a higher rate, and while families in Africa are still larger, their birth rates are also going down. I’m curious about what has caused these changes. Is it because of higher living costs, more women going to college and working, or changing ideas about family and parenthood? I also wonder how these trends will shape future generations, economies, and the balance between young and older people. This relates to my community because the cost of living keeps rising, making it harder for many families to afford having multiple children. As housing, education, and everyday expenses continue to increase, people are choosing to have fewer kids or delay starting families altogether. By the time my generation reaches the stage of having children, the birth rate will likely be even lower, as financial stability will play an even bigger role in family planning and people’s ability to raise children comfortably.
    
    A catchy title could be : How Rising Costs Are Shrinking Future Families

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I notice a graph titled with the average number of children born to a woman in different countries. The lines on the graph have gotten significantly lower from 1960 to 2020, and I believe this is because it is a lot more expensive to have as many children as compared to that of a family in the 1960s. Children then were needed to help around the house and help with outdoor work, but now they do less and cause for more money and work from the parents. Even in Mexico, whose average in 1960 was 7 children, barely averages to about 2 children per family in 2020. Women today also have more of a choice if they want to get pregnant or not compared to women in the 1960s. 
    What do you wonder?
    If inflation did not exist and children helped out more, would there still be a strong amount of families raising 5 to 7 children?
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me because what if by the time I am a parent it is normal to only have one child because of just how much work and money it is. 
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    Shrinking Families; Comparing 1960 to 2020

raw_comment:
These graphs remind me of the old saying my college history professor had.... statistics don't lie, statisticians do. 
    
    Even though birth rates globally are going down, the world population is rising.  The reason - lower infant mortality rates.  Particularly in the more advanced countries, for the last 2-3 generations, the child mortality rate has been very low.  The first generation or 2 still had multiple children out of habit, but since all of them lived, it got expensive.   The next generations had fewer children.  The children were also no longer needed as farm laborers, so the need to have 10 kids to help run the house and farm (or Alternatively go work in a factory at a young age to support the family) is no longer necessary.  
    
    This is not something to be surprised or scared of.  It is a good thing.  Less children dying and they have better childhoods in most cases.  The real headline here should be that better childhood outcomes lead to the need for less children.

raw_comment:
What do I believe from viewing this graph?
    
    Women who have access to family planning have decided to have only as many children as they can reasonably support.
    
    Women, around the world, continued since the 1960s to have more autonomy over whether they were going to get pregnant.
    
    Good thing.
    
    Especially as AI puts more people out of jobs.  Our world has been overpopulated for some time.  If we can gently decline it to a reasonable and stable number, good.

raw_comment: I notice that from 1960 to 2020, global birth rates have all declined. With minor fluctuations, there is an overall trend of women having fewer children. I observe that countries that are generally less affluent and have less infrastructure tend to have higher birth rates. Most women now opt to have only 1-2 children, with Central and Western Africa and Eastern and Southern Asia being exceptions, still having around 4-5 children. I wonder if this is directly influenced by the widespread women's rights and equality movements. Women today have more autonomy and face less social pressure to have children. These movements have also enabled women to pursue careers first and families later, which likely leads to fewer children. I also wonder if increased access to education plays a role. Girls are no longer dropping out of school to become wives and mothers; instead, they learn about sex education and contraceptives. The rise in autonomy means women can choose when to have children and have more control over their lives. I also consider whether the cost of living impacts this trend, making it less realistic to have many children and support a large family, even on two incomes. This affects me and my community because lower birth rates could lead to an underpopulation issue. From excess housing to economic consequences, a significant decrease in population size could cause many negative effects.

    2. I wonder why the fertility rate has dropped so much and whether it’s because of changes like education, cost of living, or people having kids later in life.
    3. If fewer people are having kids, it could mean smaller future classes at schools, fewer young workers, and more older people in the community. It might also affect jobs, housing, and how governments plan for the future.
    4. The Planet’s Cribs Are Emptying

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    In this graph I notice how the birth rates in different countries have been at a constant decline since the 1960s. I also notice how Mexico has the steepest decline. The countries at the bottom of the graph have more of a variation, but the birth rates are relatively the same.
    
    What do you wonder? 
    I wonder if the steep decline has to do with economical or healthcare issues, because birth and pregnancy requires a lot of time, money, and effort. I also wonder if the colors of the lines indicate anything. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because over time the population will have a drastic change. A decrease in population could also eventually lead to a shortage of people in the working class. This graph relates to me because it will be interesting to see the birth rate by the time I have reached that average age. 
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    “A Growing or Lessening Population: Each Country on their Different Path”

raw_comment:
Hi everyone!
    
    I'll be taking over the moderating for the next 2.5 hours from Moderator Jamie.  I am an AP Statistics teacher from Collinsville High School in Collinsville, Illinois just outside of St. Louis. I look forward to seeing what all you have to think about this week's graph and hope to learn something from you all!
    
    I'm going to participate with you all in this week's graph as well.
    
    What do you notice?
    I notice some countries' birth rates have had small reductions over the past 65 years while other countries have had large reductions.  
    
    What do you wonder?
    The lines with the highest birth rates are regions that make up multiple countries, so I wonder what the graph would look like instead with only individual countries. I also wonder what percentage of women not having any children has done over the past 65 years?  For my statistically minded students, I wonder what change there has been in the standard deviation in birth rates over the past 65 years.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    I wonder what the birth rates are around different regions of the US, specifically my community.  If the birth rate is too low in my area, then will fewer people around in the next generation cause strains on the local economy for businesses and more unemployment and/or will it help alleviate other strains like lack of housing?

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice a cluster of colorful lines and several lines the same grey color, each representing a different country. My attention is pulled towards the more colorful lines at the bottom, then the grey ones at the top. I also see that most of the lines are going downwards, showing a decrease in the number of children women have as the year gets more recent. 
    
    This graph makes me wonder many things. Is there a significance in the colored lines vs. the non-colored? Why has there been such a significant decrease in the amount of children each women has in recent years? Finally, I wonder for what purpose was this data recorded for? 
    
    This relates to me and my community because there may eventually start to be a low birth rate in the country. That means that the population of the country is decreasing overall. This makes me wonder about the stability of the country's economic, social, and political systems with such a dramatic decrease in birth rates. 
    
    A catchy headline for this could be: "A Decrease in Birthrates Worldwide".

raw_comment: In this graph I notice many different graph lines representing the average number of children each woman has in several different countries. Countries like France, United States, Norway, Hungary, and Canada all have around the same average of two children per woman. I notice that Hungary had dipped the lowest out of all the countries to about one child, but has now increased to around two. I also see that Mexico in the early 60’s had one of the highest amounts, at seven children per one woman. However now it has almost exactly two children per woman. I wonder why Mexico had such a drastic drop in the last decades. I also wonder why some of the rate lines are in grey and not bolded in color like the others. For instance Countries like France, United States, Norway, Hungary, Mexico, and Canada are all colored and bolded. While regions like South Asia and Central & Western Africa lines are light grey and thin. Could it possibly be because they are regions and not countries? This relates to me because I am a woman myself and it is interesting how the numbers change frequently, so by the time I am older the average children may be lower or much higher. It also affects the community because it changes the population and birth rate per year. To conclude a catchy headline for this graph could be, “Why is your population that number?”

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice
    
    I notice that in the 20th century, countries such as Mexico, the Middle East and North Africa, Central and Western Africa, South Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean had around 6-7 children. I noticed that East Asia and the Pacific had an increase in children per woman, from 4 to 6, followed by a decrease to 3. I noticed the US, France, Norway, and Hungary had around 2-3 kids and kept it at a constant rate. The other countries ranged from 3-4 kids and went down to around 2-3. 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder why a few countries had a lot of kids to begin with, compared to other countries that had half or fewer (Mexico compared to Hungary). Why did Mexico's rates decline so much after a period of time? Are Gen Z and Gen Alpha the most declined in rates of offspring? Why do central and western Africa and eastern and southern Africa have the highest fertility rates? 
    
    
    3. How does this relate to your community?
    
    This relates to my community and me because we have a serious population decline. One of the many reasons is abortions and having millions of “babies missing” or not born. This can affect us because, as the years go on, we will only continue to decline, and the business,  for instance, will decline in numbers because of fewer people. With a big decline in numbers, the population will not be stable. 
    
    4. Create a catchy title
    
    Baby deficit; It's a kid-trastophe!

raw_comment:
1. In this graph, you can see the number of children born per woman in countries and how it has changed from 1960-2020. It is clearly visible, that in the less economically developed countries, the amount of children per woman is relatively high compared to the others. Over time, the average amount of children has decreased in almost all selected countries. The steepest curve with the most drastic drop is from Mexico, where the average amount in 1960 was almost 7 children, which caused for Mexico to be one of the countries with the highest amount of children per woman, although, in the timespan from 1960 to 2020, the curve has dropped all the way to <2 children, which made Mexico’s current birth rate align with many MEDC’s (more economically developed countries) like France, Norway or the US.
    
    2+3. I wonder, if the overpopulation on our planet will decrease over time, since the birth rates are also decreasing quite steadily in most areas of the world. Also, what if the dropping birth rate in the MEDC’s  will cause for the LEDC’s to become overpopulated with the vast majority of all people living there? Might this be a new trigger for global capitalism? Or maybe the large amount of people in the LEDC’s will help the countries develop more, so in the future the economical roles of the countries get switched?
    
    4. Title Ideas: Does our global overpopulation have a chance of healing? 
    Will the dropping birth rates in MEDC’s cause a wave of global capitalism?

raw_comment:
I notice that, from 1960 to 2020, all examined countries and regions underwent declines in the average number of children born per mother. Mexico showed the most significant drop (from about 6.8 in 1960 to about 1.8 in 2020), with the steepest decline recorded from around 1972 to 1986. The same pattern could be seen in the Middle East and North Africa, with the steepest decline taking place a decade later. In stark contrast, the Central & Western Africa and Eastern & Southern Africa regions experienced a relatively mild decrease, from 6.5 to slightly below 5 and from 6.8 to 4.2, respectively, retaining their leading positions throughout the period. Meanwhile, figures from the US, Canada, and several EU countries remained at the bottom, hovering around 1.5-2 children per mother in 2020.

raw_comment:
Fewer babies are being born, but the population is going up. How? (headline)
    
    I noticed that over time, the average number of babies a mother has in each country decreases. This could happen because the cost of having a child rose over time and because of inflation. I wonder if the reason is actually because of the state that the world is in, or if it is because of the people; maybe adults want to have fewer kids, or no kids at all. This relates to me and my community very little; my mom and dad have 6 kids, including me, and our neighbors have 2 or more kids, if married. So this data does make me see that other families don't have many kids, and it could be quieter in their houses. But lots of my friends have either one sibling or none, so it's also not that surprising.

This leaves Switzerland largely demographically stable, despite low birth rate.
